patient.chief_complaint: Progressive behavioral changes and personality shift — 18 months; referred from primary care after disability evaluation
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. R is a 57-year-old elementary school teacher currently on disability leave who presents to the cognitive neurology clinic with an 18-month history of progressive behavioral and personality changes, reported primarily by her adult daughter who accompanied her. Ms. R herself minimizes her difficulties and states that she 'just needs more rest.' Her daughter describes a woman who was formerly a dedicated and beloved teacher — organized, nurturing, and highly regarded in her community — who has undergone a profound transformation. Over the past 18 months, Ms. R has become increasingly impulsive, spending significant sums on online shopping without financial awareness or apparent concern. She has shown reduced empathy, repeatedly failing to acknowledge her daughter's distress during difficult life events and laughing at inappropriate times. She repeats the same short phrases and stories in conversation, often circling back to the same anecdote within minutes. She has been collecting cheap figurines in a compulsive fashion, filling her apartment with hundreds of identical items. She stopped attending her church, which she had done every Sunday for 35 years. Her grooming and hygiene have declined and her daughter must remind her to shower and change clothes. She was placed on disability leave 6 months ago after school parents and administrators raised concerns about her classroom behavior — she was reportedly making inappropriate personal comments to students and parents. Her episodic memory has also declined — she does not recall that her daughter was engaged until reminded, despite being told multiple times. Her brother died of ALS at age 60 six years ago. She is unaware of any genetic link between ALS and dementia.

results.title: A hexanucleotide repeat expansion in C9ORF72 is the cause of chromosome 9p21-linked ALS-FTD
C9orf72 repeat expansion in familial and sporadic ALS-FTD

output.summary: C9orf72 GGGGCC hexanucleotide repeat expansion (>30 repeats; typically >400 in disease) is the most common genetic cause of familial FTD (25-40% of familial FTD) and familial ALS (40% of familial ALS). Key clinical points: (1) autosomal dominant with high but incomplete penetrance; (2) each first-degree child has 50% risk; (3) can present as FTD, ALS, or combined FTD-ALS in different family members; (4) anticipatory grief and family testing disclosure require genetic counselor involvement; (5) no disease-modifying therapy currently approved but ASO trials targeting C9orf72 are in Phase 1-2 trials. Pre-symptomatic testing of family members requires formal genetic counseling.

useless_tools.rationale: EEG is non-specific in FTD; not part of the standard dementia workup unless seizures or rapidly progressive course suggest CJD or autoimmune encephalitis.
ECG has no role in the cognitive workup of suspected FTD; reserved for syncope, palpitations, or pre-procedure clearance.
Echocardiography is unrelated to a neurodegenerative cognitive syndrome and adds cost without diagnostic value.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is unrelated to FTD and not indicated absent syncope or palpitations.
Non-contrast head CT lacks the resolution and lobar specificity needed to characterise frontotemporal atrophy; MRI is the standard structural study.
MR spectroscopy has no established role in the routine FTD diagnostic pathway.
Perfusion MRI is not indicated in the standard FTD workup once a structural MRI and FDG-PET (or amyloid PET) have characterised the lobar pattern.
Carotid duplex is a vascular study with no diagnostic role in primary neurodegenerative dementia.
DaTscan evaluates presynaptic dopaminergic terminals; it is not indicated unless overt parkinsonism raises concern for PD, DLB, or atypical parkinsonism (PSP/CBS overlap).

sequence_constraints.reason: Exclude structural cause of focal cognitive symptoms and screen for elevated ICP before lumbar puncture.

critical_actions: Pursue genetic testing — high pre-test probability for C9orf72 given family history of ALS.
Provide formal genetic counselling and discuss cascade testing for adult relatives.
Establish baseline motor / respiratory function to detect emerging ALS features.
Apply Rascovsky 2011 bvFTD criteria explicitly (≥3 of 6 core features within 3 years) and document functional decline.
Assess and document decision-making, financial, and driving capacity given the high risk of impulsivity and impaired judgment in FTD.
Provide caregiver education, safety planning, and referral to FTD-focused support resources.
Offer genetic counselling and discuss cascade testing options if a pathogenic variant is identified or suspected.
contraindicated_actions: Do not start acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine): no benefit in FTD and may worsen behavioral symptoms.
Do not start memantine: no evidence of benefit in bvFTD and may worsen behavioral symptoms.
Avoid antipsychotics as first-line behavioral therapy given increased cerebrovascular and mortality risk in dementia; reserve for refractory dangerous agitation with specialist oversight.
Avoid benzodiazepines for behavioral control: risk of paradoxical disinhibition and falls.
key_reasoning_points: Brother with ALS + behavioural / cognitive syndrome → C9orf72 must be considered until excluded.
Mother's 'nervous breakdown' is more likely an early FTD/C9orf72 manifestation than primary psychiatric illness.
Symmetric upper-extremity rigidity is not parkinsonism warranting DaTscan; the lobar FTD pattern is the diagnostic finding.

red_herrings.intended_effect: Could be mistaken for primary psychiatric inheritance.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Late-life personality / psychiatric change in a relative of a C9orf72 carrier is most likely an early FTD manifestation.

metadata.notes: Moderate bvFTD — C9orf72-positive with family history of ALS. Key teaching: ALS family history mandates C9orf72 testing; same expansion causes FTD-ALS spectrum phenotype. Borderline hippocampal MRI creates diagnostic ambiguity resolved by FDG-PET and amyloid PET.
